description: Wings exact to the last scale, a lantern-sized dragon guessed at, and a jet of flame three times its length.
lore: Somebody told this one into existence, though not on purpose and not by themselves. No dragon was ever anywhere to be remembered; what there was, in a hundred countries at once, was the telling of one, and a telling said often enough to enough people who were listening weighs as much here as a life does. So what pooled in this case was not the memory of an animal. It was the memory of an account of one, and you can see the difference from ten paces. Whoever did most of the remembering had never seen a dragon, which is unremarkable, since no one has. They had seen a meadow in summer. They had lain in it and watched the irises being worked over, close up, for as long as a child watches anything, and when the account ran out — and an account is mostly the places where it runs out — that was what came to hand. The wings are accordingly the best-made thing about the creature: four of them, violet banded through with pink, exact to the last scale. The body is stubby, grey-green and only approximately a lizard. What somebody actually looked at comes out sharp. What they took on trust comes out roughly.

Then it opens its mouth and puts out a jet of flame three times its own length, and the joke stops there. That part is not vague. The fire is the one detail that survives every retelling in every country whose dead are here, so it came through whole and unworn, entirely indifferent to the fact that the thing carrying it is the size of a lantern. Being wrong about a creature does not make the creature harmless. It only decides which parts of it are.

The oddity, and stone-workers will raise it before you have finished asking, is that a creature this full of fire does not put down a fire stone. Knocked down, it goes up in its own flame, and at the very end the flame stops being orange. It turns violet — the colour of the wings, the colour of the one summer that actually got looked at — and what sits in the ash afterwards is violet too, faceted all over, with a small gold mark set at the middle of it like something written down. Carried, it lands a blow with the weight of a thing recalled rather than a thing swung, and it brings whatever you have just done back to your hand faster than you could fetch it yourself. The Chroniclers make a good deal of that mark. The tellers let them have it, and then point out that the only part of this creature anybody anywhere can be relied on to have is the fire, which is not the part that lasted. Both sides go home satisfied, which is usual.

It has no hoard. Where a dragon keeps one was never clear to anybody; that it has one was, so the having came through and the where did not. What it does instead is both halves of itself at once, without ever noticing that they do not go together: it sits out on the warm black rock as though guarding something, with nothing under it to guard, and then comes down to the meadow irises and works them over the way the thing whose wings it has would, and goes away trailing petals it has no use for. It cannot want the hoard. There is no one in it to want with. It is only doing, very carefully, what it was assembled out of.
